**The Last Letter**

I found it tucked between the pages of an old, leather-bound book—yellowed with time, the edges frayed as if it had been read a hundred times before. The letter was addressed to me, though I had never written to it. The handwriting was neat, almost childlike, though the tone was anything but.

*"Dear Future Me,"* it began, *"I hope you’re doing well. I’m writing this in the year 2045, and I wanted to tell you something important. The world has changed in ways you can’t even imagine. The oceans are rising, the air is thick with smoke, and the last of the old forests are gone. But here’s the thing—we didn’t destroy ourselves. We fixed it. Not perfectly, but enough. We learned to live in balance, to listen to the earth instead of dominating it. And you? You were part of it. You carried the knowledge of the past, the wisdom of the old ways, and you helped us remember what was lost. So thank you. For everything."*

I set the letter down, my fingers still trembling. The book was a copy of *The Last Journal of Dr. Eleanor Voss*, a botanist who had spent her life studying the last remaining ancient trees. The letter was dated 2045, but the journal was from 2023. How had it gotten here? Had someone left it for me, or was it a message from the future?

I flipped through the journal, the pages filled with sketches of dying forests, notes on climate models, and a single, handwritten note: *"If you’re reading this, it means I was wrong. The trees weren’t just dying—they were fighting back. And you? You were the one who saw it."*

The last entry was dated December 2023. The world had ended that year. Not with fire or flood, but with silence. The last of the ancient trees had died, and with them, something else. Something that had been keeping the world alive.

I closed the book, the weight of it pressing against my chest. The letter was real. The journal was real. And the future had sent it to me—because I was the only one who could understand it.

Because I was the last one who remembered.

Because I was the last one who could listen.
